units.text: Reward and the Promise of Reward

A guaranteed prize has a narrative drawback: its story is already over. A possible prize still calls for an action. This difference does not automatically make uncertainty irrational. But it forces us to separate the value of the prize from the experience of pursuing it.

In four studies with real rewards, Shen, Fishbach, and Hsee found situations in which participants invested more resources in an uncertain reward than in a certain one with a higher expected value. The effect depended on attention being directed toward the process of pursuit rather than the final outcome. This is not a law saying people always prefer risk; it is an observation about how uncertainty can make pursuit more engaging. [1]
When Anticipation Is Part of the Gain

There are activities in which anticipation is precisely what we buy. At a match, we do not merely want to read the score. With a mystery, we do not necessarily ask for the last paragraph. Play need not be justified by delivering a monetizable skill. Its pleasure can be enough.

This defense of play matters. Otherwise, the book would become a manual for morally accounting for every minute. Not every long evening of exploration is an evening wasted. The problem is not that we enjoy ourselves. The problem is that we can call entertainment “proven research,” affirmation “truth,” and filling time “productivity” without noticing the shift in category.

Suppose Mara asks the model for ten analogies for an intuition. She receives one beautiful analogy and nine conventional ones. She continues and gets another interesting one. The activity may be useful. But if she begins evaluating the theory by the frequency of moments of wonder, she has changed the criterion. Wonder is a real experience. The theory’s validity is a different question.
Almost: A Word That Needs Explaining

At a target, a projectile close to the center can inform the next adjustment. In a lottery, a number close to the winning one does not bring us closer to the next win in the same sense. Visual resemblance between two outcomes does not have the same value in every mechanism.

The literature on the “near miss,” an almost-winning outcome, requires more caution than popular explanations suggest. Pisklak, Yong, and Spetch showed that subjective or physiological reactions do not automatically establish increased persistence in gambling. Their analysis and experiments did not support a robust behavioral effect under the conditions tested. This does not prove the absence of any effect in every context; it does, however, constrain the overly simple story in which “almost” inevitably compels continuation. [5]

For LLM use, we propose an analogy rather than transferring a clinical or experimental conclusion: some answers seem very close to success without providing a real measure of that closeness. We will call this the “semantic near miss.”

An elegant explanation can have the wrong premise. A paper can have impeccable sections and nonexistent data. Code can pass every example presented and miss the one condition that matters in operation. Sometimes a small correction really is all that is needed. At other times, the almost-perfect surface conceals a structural problem.
Why the Dopamine Explanation Is Too Short

Saying that “dopamine makes us press again” does not explain the difference between a curious reader, a persevering researcher, and someone who can no longer stop despite the consequences. Curiosity research examines mechanisms of valuation, learning, and anticipation; merely invoking a neurotransmitter does not produce a complete theory of the activity. [2]

It is more useful to ask what reward the person is pursuing and what information they receive. A student who keeps trying until they understand is not doing the same thing as one who regenerates until a solution appears that can be copied. From the outside, the gestures may look alike. From within the learning process, their consequences differ.
The Promise That Never Runs Out

A machine has a limited number of symbols. Language can invent a new form of promise after almost every failure. If the solution does not work, a more general theory can appear. If the theory is vague, a memorable name can appear. If the name fails to convince, a vision of the future can appear.

These transformations can be creative. They become a trap when the new promise erases the obligation to evaluate the old one. This book will not recommend eliminating hope. It will recommend not using it as a unit of truth.
